passages.t: The two kings east of the Jordan
passages.happening:
The story pauses, and the writer makes a list. It begins on the far side of the river, with the kings defeated before Israel crossed.

There were two. Sihon, king of the Amorites, lived in Heshbon and ruled the country from the Arnon Valley north to the Jabbok River (verses 2-3). Og, king of Bashan, ruled the land north of that, as far as Mount Hermon (verses 4-5).

“Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the Israelites had struck them down and given their land as an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
This chapter closes the first half of the book. The wars are over. Before the land is divided, the writer stops to count what God has done.

He starts with Moses. The victories over Sihon and Og were won at the end of the wilderness years, before Moses died, and they are told in Numbers and Deuteronomy. By putting them first, the writer joins the work of Moses and the work of Joshua into one story. Joshua did not begin something new. He carried on what God had started under Moses.

These two victories were among the best remembered in Israel. Rahab named them when she spoke to the scouts. The Gibeonites named them. Israel sang about them in its worship.

The Arnon is a deep river valley that runs into the Dead Sea from the east. The Jabbok joins the Jordan further north. Mount Hermon stands in the far north. Between those points lay the high country east of the Jordan, good land for herds, which the two and a half tribes had asked for.

The word ‘inheritance’ in verse 6 looks ahead. The second half of the book is about land received as a family's share and held as a gift.
passages.later:
Israel's worship kept these names: “Sihon king of the Amorites” and “and Og king of Bashan”, each answered with the line, “His loving devotion endures forever” (Psalm 136:19-20).

The wars themselves are told in Numbers 21 and again in Deuteronomy 2 and 3. The notes on those chapters set out how Christians read their language of total destruction.
passages.asks: Before moving on, the writer stopped and counted what God had done, going back to things that happened under another leader. Ask what God did in your life, or in your church, before the present chapter began. Ask whether you have written any of it down. And ask whose work you are carrying on, and whether you have thanked God for them.

passages.happening:
Now the list crosses the river. These are the kings whom Joshua and Israel defeated west of the Jordan, from the far north to the far south (verse 7).

Then come the names, each followed by the same single word. ‘the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is near Bethel, one’ (verse 9). The king of Jerusalem, one. The king of Hebron, one. The list runs on through the towns of the south and then the towns of the north, Hazor among them.

It ends with a total: “So there were thirty-one kings in all” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
A modern reader may wonder how so small a land could hold thirty-one kings. Canaan in this age was not one country. It was a patchwork of small city-states. Each ‘king’ here was the ruler of one walled town with the villages and fields around it.

Kings in the ancient world kept lists like this. The pharaohs of Egypt had the names of the towns they claimed to have conquered carved on temple walls. A list was a public record of victory.

In Israel the list also worked as a kind of worship. The Hebrew word ‘one’ is repeated after every name. It turns the record into a count, and the count builds: one, one, one, up to thirty-one. A reader is meant to feel how much was done. And all through the book it has been said who did it. These many kings, each a power in his own place, fell before one LORD.

The names follow the order of the story. Jericho and Ai come first, then the kings of the southern campaign, then the north. Some towns in the list became important later in Israel's history. Megiddo guarded the main pass into the great northern valley. Tirzah was for a time the capital of the northern kingdom.

A reader should not picture thirty-one burned cities. The book has named only three cities as burned. This is a list of kings defeated, and the hard question below looks at what that does and does not mean.
passages.later:
The New Testament speaks of a victory over powers greater than any of these, and it locates that victory in an unexpected place: “And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross” (Colossians 2:15).

It also speaks of an inheritance that no later defeat can take away: ‘an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you’ (1 Peter 1:4).
passages.hard:
If all these kings were defeated, why do later chapters say that many of their cities were still in Canaanite hands?

The book itself raises the question. Jerusalem, Gezer, Megiddo, Taanach and Dor are all in this list. Each appears later as a town Israel did not take or did not hold (Joshua 15:63; 16:10; 17:11-12; Judges 1:27).

Readers answer in three ways. Many note that defeating a king is not the same as settling his city. A king could die in battle while his town lived on, was taken up again by its people, or was never occupied by Israel. Others read the list as a summary in the usual sweeping style of ancient victory records, which the book itself goes on to qualify. Others think the book draws on sources with different emphases.

These notes do not choose. The book seems aware of the tension. The very next chapter opens with God saying to Joshua that ‘very much of the land remains to be possessed’ (Joshua 13:1).
passages.asks: The list says ‘one’ thirty-one times. Ask what it would look like to count the things God has done for you one at a time, and not in a general way. Then read the verse from Colossians again. Ask which powers hold people captive in the place where you live, such as fear, debt, addiction or contempt, and what it would mean to believe that Christ has already triumphed over them.
